title: SSDP discovery
source: UPnP Device Architecture 1.1 §1.3; RFC 7230 §3 for the syntax it borrows

about: SSDP — UPnP Device Architecture 1.1 §1.3, which is HTTP 1.1's syntax over UDP multicast to
239.255.255.250:1900 and no TCP anywhere.
The opposite of every other protocol here, and that is why it is in the corpus. There is not one
length field, not one fixed width, and not one number written as a number. Every span in both
captures ends because a separator begins — a space, a colon, or a carriage return and a line
feed — and the run of headers ends at a line with nothing on it.
Which needs no field kind of its own. A span with no width, followed by a node whose value is a
constant, runs up to where that constant starts: the separator stays the next node's own value,
so it is written back out by the thing that owns it, and a description can name it and check it
like anything else. Nothing is copied into a declaration and nothing is consumed twice.
A header's value is carried EXACTLY as written, including the space after the colon that most of
them have and EXT: has not. RFC 7230 §3.2 calls that optional whitespace and says it is not part
of the value; this description keeps it anyway, because a datagram that arrived with one space
and went out with none is a different datagram and SSDP has no length field that would notice.
Trimming it is the caller's, exactly as reading MX's ' 3' as a number is.
What a description can REFUSE here is almost nothing, and that is a finding rather than an
omission. Everything after a separator is text, so there is no width to disagree with, no length
to contradict and no reserved bit to be set wrongly. The one thing the octets can be held to is
the start line: eight characters that say M-SEARCH or HTTP/1.1 and nothing else, which is how a
NOTIFY — ssdp:alive and ssdp:byebye, the unsolicited half of SSDP that no request precedes — is
refused where it is written rather than read as a search with peculiar headers.

nodes.about: One start line, some headers, and a blank line. UPnP 1.1 §1.1.2 requires the blank line and forbids a body, so the datagram ends there.

nodes.label: a space
nodes.about: RFC 7230 §3.1.1 separates a start line's three tokens with exactly one.

nodes.label: a colon
nodes.about: What ends a header's name. The FIRST one — a value may hold as many more as it likes, and HOST: and LOCATION: both do.

nodes.label: a carriage return and a line feed
nodes.about: What ends every line. Two characters, and a description that ended a line at the line feed alone would leave the carriage return at the front of the next one.

about: RFC 7230 §3.1 gives two shapes and they are the same three tokens: a request-line is a method, a
target and a version; a status-line is a version, a code and a phrase. Three spans, two spaces.
Told apart by looking, because nothing has been read yet — this IS the first octet. Eight
characters is enough and is exactly enough: M-SEARCH and HTTP/1.1 are both eight long, so the
look-ahead is one span rather than a rule about how far to read.
There is no `otherwise`. A start line that is neither is refused by there being no way on, which
is what states the scope: NOTIFY * HTTP/1.1 is SSDP's other half and is a different message.

nodes.about: Read ahead of deciding, from a copy of the position. Nothing is consumed, and the message that gets chosen reads its own first token from its own first octet.

nodes.purpose: M-SEARCH for a search, HTTP/1.1 for an answer. It is both the fork and the first token — the same fact, so the same input, rather than a discriminator beside a field that repeats it and can disagree with it.

nodes.about: UPnP 1.1 §1.3.2. The method is M-SEARCH, the target is a bare asterisk because there is no resource being addressed, and the version is the one HTTP this speaks.

UPnP 1.1 §1.3.3. Sent by unicast back to wherever the search came from, after waiting a random part of MX seconds so that a hundred devices do not answer at once — which is a rule about when to send rather than about what a datagram is.
M-SEARCH, and it is the same characters the fork looked at. Read from this node's own first octet regardless — a place never has to know that something looked before choosing it.

nodes.purpose: A bare asterisk in every M-SEARCH there has ever been: UPnP 1.1 §1.3.2 has no resource to name, and the request-line has to have a target because HTTP says so.

nodes.about: The status line's first token, which is the version — where the request line's is the method. Same position, different thing, which is why the fork is on shapes rather than on a field's value.

nodes.purpose: 200, as characters. Every number in this protocol is decimal text, so reading it as a number is the caller's — and 200 written as 0200 would be a different datagram.
OK. RFC 7230 §3.1.2 lets it hold spaces, which is why it runs to the end of the line rather than to the next separator.

nodes.as: the end of the start line
nodes.about: One node reached from both shapes, because both end the same way — and it is what says where the third token stops, whichever of the two that token is.

about: One per line, and how many there are is written nowhere: not counted, not bounded, and not
guessable from anything in front of them. The run ends at a line with nothing on it, which the
reading finds by looking at two characters before committing to another header.
Kept in the order they arrived. UPnP does not care about the order and this description does,
because a datagram that came in one way and went out another is a different datagram — and here
there is no length field anywhere that would notice the difference.

nodes.purpose: One record per header line, in wire order. The value is what lies between the colon and the end of the line, whitespace and all.

nodes.about: Up to the first colon. UPnP 1.1 §1.1.2 makes these case-insensitive and every device writes them in capitals; carried as written, because folding them would make the answer a different datagram from the one that arrived.

about: Everything between the colon and the end of the line, exactly as written.
Which is why EXT: is here at all. It is a header whose value is nothing — no space, no
characters — and it means something: UPnP 1.1 §1.3.3 requires it, and it is how a device says
it understood the MAN header. Present and empty, and a description that trimmed or defaulted
would make it indistinguishable from absent.

nodes.about: What ends the headers, and it is a line with nothing on it rather than a sentinel beside the run — the same two characters that end every header, at a point where no header began.

nodes.as: another header, or the blank line?
about: Two characters, unconsumed. A carriage return and a line feed here is the blank line; anything
else is the start of another header's name.
The same shape as the end of a DNS name, where a length of zero is the root — and for the same
reason, which is that the terminator is not a sentinel put beside the run. It is the run's own
line ending occurring where a name would have been.

nodes.about: Read from a copy of the position, so whichever way this goes reads from where the walk already is.
UPnP 1.1 §1.1.2: the blank line ends the message and there is no body. A reading with octets still in hand has found something this does not describe.
